what: Every resource bound on the path SDK admission -> Torii -> queue -> VM -> proposer -> block -> RS16 payload -> transport, frame and sync -> follower validation -> storage, with its value today, its single code owner, where it is enforced, how it is classed and the relations that must hold between bounds. The checker reads every owner from the source and fails on drift. `completeness` names the owner files, directories and committed-parameter modules the checker scans: a limit defined there is a bound here or is excluded with a reason. `catalogs` checks the node-local validity limits against the two typed catalogs of node configuration the code owns (the execution-policy digest and the Nexus consensus-policy preimage) and the committed limits against the committed ZK validity policy (the ZK consensus-policy hash inventory, moved into committed State by task F.4) and the two committed policy structs. `pin_tests` names the tests that only pin a value or a digest projection: a consensus bound backed by nothing else records the task that owns its boundary test.

classes.consensus: Deterministic consensus bound. Every validator derives the same accept or reject decision from committed State or a compile-time protocol constant. A validity-affecting bound whose source is node-local configuration is a defect with an owning task.
classes.local_defer: Local resource. Exhausting it defers or refuses one local attempt; it never rejects a transaction or block, casts a vote or changes an accepted effect, gas or certified root.
classes.engineering_target: Engineering time or memory target measured on named hardware. It guides construction, is compared with an observation only and is never validity.
classes.local_schedule: Local scheduling limit. A time budget a node plans or waits within, including a committed parameter used that way. Exceeding it retries or re-plans one local attempt; it never rejects a transaction or block, casts a vote or changes an accepted effect, gas or certified root, and it is not a performance target.

sources.committed: Genesis or State parameter; the owner is its default.
sources.node_local: Node configuration or a node-local default.

fields.owner: The single definition the checker reads: file, symbol, kind (const, fn, field or arm), optional anchors applied in order and the defining expression. `refs` maps a constant the expression names to the bound that owns it.
fields.enforcement: Where the bound is compared or applied, by stage. A site that is only a symbol, a constant definition or a function signature is rejected. `count` is how many times the text occurs in the file when that is not one; a different number is drift.
fields.tests: Active Rust or Python tests of the bound (`macro` names a macro_rules! generator, `macro_path` the file that defines it when the test file is an include of it). A test that is ignored, compiled out, without #[test] or in a file no module path of its crate reaches is rejected.
fields.test_gap: The task that owns the missing boundary test of a consensus bound. The bound names no test, or only tests listed in `pin_tests`.
fields.test_note: What the named tests do and do not cover.
fields.unenforced: A value bound into consensus State that no state transition compares anything with; the owner task enforces or removes it. `observations` may name a local service that compares it.
fields.defect: Why a validity-affecting bound read from node configuration is a defect, with its owner task.
fields.catalog: The field of an authoritative typed catalog in the code this node-local bound mirrors.
fields.observations: Where something is compared with the bound outside consensus validity: a measured value as evidence, or the own check of a local service for a bound recorded `unenforced`.
fields.zero_means: What the value zero means for this bound.
fields.inclusive: Whether the bound itself is admitted.
fields.framing: Which encoding overhead a byte length includes.
fields.fixed: The delivery plan keeps this value; the checker holds an independent copy.
fields.value_pin: Why a pin of the value is the right test of a bound whose every test is in `pin_tests`.

stage_decisions.what: How the stages decide on the size of one transaction, from committed parameters only.
stage_decisions.sdk: Parameters::check_signed_transaction_bytes(bytes, route): at most min(max_tx_bytes, the largest selection budget on the route). TransactionInclusionRoute::Global is max_block_bytes - 65,536 and is sufficient on every route; NativeLane { max_block_bytes } adds that lane's max_block_bytes - 64 and holds only for a transaction the committed routing rules send to that lane.
stage_decisions.torii: AcceptedTransaction admission: at most max_tx_bytes; then the queue.
stage_decisions.queue: Queue::prepare_checked_for_enqueue: the bound of the transaction's route at the admission height. A transaction routed to lane zero has the global budget; one routed to a native lane also has the budget of that lane's committed record (the payload limit its proposer builds within, pinned when the lane was created). Above it the transaction is refused as UnsupportedTransactionAdmission with the actual and permitted bytes. An unreadable committed policy or route defers the assessment (Error::Deferred) and takes no custody.
stage_decisions.proposer: payload::select: at most min(max_transactions, FASTPQ Network input cap) own transactions within max_block_bytes - 65,536, including the rescue of an input whose lane has stalled; the lane builder selects within the lane's max_block_bytes - 64 and compares the encoded batch with the lane's max_block_bytes; then the assembled proposal wire within max_block_bytes.
stage_decisions.follower: Signed header payload_len <= max_block_bytes and every transaction <= max_tx_bytes. The follower accepts every block an honest proposer builds. The proposer's reserve is packing policy, not a validity rule: a block around a transaction inside the reserve window is valid if built.
stage_decisions.agreement: Where transaction_cap_fits_block_payload holds, every stage accepts exactly the transactions of at most max_tx_bytes. Where it does not (today's defaults), admission is stricter than block validity by the reserve, so nothing admitted is larger than the selection budget of a proposer on its route at the admission height. That is not a promise of inclusion for a lane-routed transaction above the global budget: only its lane's proposer can carry it. The global rescue selects within the global budget and skips it, so if the lane stalls or closes, or the routing rules stop sending the transaction to that lane, it stays queued until it expires.

A maximum zk-X509 proof must be carriable as an inline signed-transaction attachment (delivery plan, 'One-call API and IVM composition'). One occurrence holds exactly the proof ceiling as raw proof bytes, the attachment frame adds a 64 KiB allowance for the descriptor and all framing, and the complete signed transaction with such a proof is measured within the 10 MiB transaction cap. The former 8 MiB proof attachment list is no longer a transaction field.

The attachment frame is part of the framed signed transaction, so its bound cannot exceed the transaction cap. The margin is what remains for the signatures, the executable and the other payload fields beside a maximal attachment frame.

The attachment frame bound is one ceiling-sized occurrence plus a fixed 64 KiB aggregate allowance for the descriptor and all Norito framing, so the byte bound and the occurrence count are independent: two maximal occurrences already exceed it.
A ceiling-sized native proof travels as exactly one occurrence of raw proof bytes; the occurrence bound is neither below the separately fixed proof ceiling nor a second, larger ceiling.
A signed contract invocation binding names a call path the host can follow: its depth bound equals the nested contract-call depth the IVM host admits.

The bounded proof attachment list of the prover API and of SDK staging is 1,114,112 bytes below the signed attachment frame bound. Carrying each of at most sixteen staged attachments as one transaction-level proof carrier adds a 40-byte frame header and a fixed-size declaration per attachment, far less than that margin, so a staged list is not refused by the signed attachment frame bound for its size.
Each staged proof attachment becomes one signed attachment occurrence, so the list holds exactly as many attachments as a transaction carries occurrences.
The list count is documented as matching the governed zk.max_verify_batch default; a batch the verifier accepts must be carriable in one list.
The governed Time invocation count must remain within the committed execution-output capacity envelope.
One output row fits the block's output total, the total fits the executed wire, and the committed wire bound never exceeds the protocol ceiling.
One entry fits the block source and one mandatory obligation fits one entry, which is what FastpqSourcePolicyV1::maximum_network_inputs requires before it sizes a block.

Under the default policies the FASTPQ source policy, not max_transactions, decides how many transactions a block carries: eleven. A workload plan that assumes 512 transactions per block is wrong until the source policy is resized.

The proof establishes CRL validity for the complete window, so a window wider than the CRL-age bound would admit a stale CRL at its end. The two are validity bounds; x509.prover_target_seconds is an engineering target with the same value and is in no relation with them.

completeness.what: The owner files, directories and committed-parameter modules the checker scans. In a `const` scope every constant, and every immutable `static`, whose name marks a limit (MAX, MAXIMUM, LIMIT, BUDGET, CEILING, OVERHEAD, RESERVE, CAP or CAPACITY) is in scope; in a `default_fn` scope every default of the module is. A `tree` scope scans every Rust source below a directory, test, bench, example and fixture files and the paths under `skip` excepted, so a new file there is scanned too. Each limit is the owner of a bound above or is excluded here with the reason it is not a resource bound of the transaction and proof path, and an excluded limit records its defining expression in `exprs`: the reason was written for that value, so a changed value fails the checker until the exclusion is reviewed and refreshed. A new limit in a scanned file fails the checker until it is classified, a second definition of a listed name fails it, and every file that owns a constant bound is scanned. The crates on the path are scanned whole: the data model (iroha_data_model), Torii (iroha_torii), the node (iroha_core) and the proof-verification crate (iroha_core_zk), with the consensus core, the IVM and its ABI and the P2P layer. In the four crates named first (`comparisons`) a limit is also found by what the code compares, whatever its name: an integer constant that takes part in a relational comparison (`<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, also written as the methods `.lt`, `.le`, `.gt`, `.ge`), in a capping call (`.min`, `.max`, `.clamp`, `.take`, `.truncate`), in either of the two called as a function, bare or behind any path (`cmp::max(a, b)`, `u32::clamp(n, 2, 64)`, `PartialOrd::lt(&a, &b)`), or in a range tested with `.contains`, the tested value included. A call compares its arguments and, for `.min`, `.max`, `.clamp` and the comparison methods, its receiver: the whole method chain in front of the call, on one line or broken across several (`ROWS.min(n)`, `n.saturating_mul(ROWS).saturating_add(1).min(cap)`). Also: an integer constant that the defining expression of a scanned limit names (a term of that limit, followed until no new constant appears); a limit-named function without parameters that returns an integer, an `Option` of one or a `Result` of one; and every literal comparison (`literals`), whether the literal is a whole operand or a part of one. An excluded term records under `term_of` the limits it is part of. A source whose name looks like a test or fixture file is scanned when its crate compiles it outside test builds; a source that every declaration gates by `cfg(test)` is read by name only. An inline module is test code when one of its `cfg` gates holds only in test builds, in whatever order the gate is written (`all(feature = "..", test)`), and its block is read on the code alone, so a brace in a character literal or a raw string of the tests hides nothing that follows the module. `python3 scripts/check_zk_resource_contract.py --mutate` changes every scanned limit and every literal of every recorded comparison in memory, one at a time, and fails when a change goes unnoticed. What no textual scan sees is stated in the checker's documentation and in specs/zk_first_release_goals.md: a limit that reaches its comparison only through a function argument, a struct field or a local variable and is neither limit-named nor compared by name; a limit a function returns when the function takes parameters, its name has no limit word or its return type is no integer, `Option` of one or `Result` of one; a limit computed at run time; a constant of a non-integer type (a `Duration`, a range), or an integer typed through a type alias, that its name does not mark; a literal below `literals.minimum` or that is no integer. Comparisons the scan does not read, for a constant that no name marks as for a literal: one with `==`, `!=`, `cmp` or `partial_cmp`; a `match` pattern; a range test written as a function (`RangeInclusive::contains`); a relational operator written without whitespace around it; checked arithmetic that refuses by underflow (`limit.checked_sub(64)?`); the receiver of `.take` and `.truncate` (the collection that is cut, as in `(0..ROWS).take(n)`); what a block yields when the block is the receiver of a cap or an operand (`match kind { .. }.min(cap)`); the head of a receiver chain in front of a blank outside brackets (the first arguments of a turbofish, as in `rows::<A, B>().min(cap)`); a cap or comparison function called under another name (an alias of `use`); and a constant or literal further than 600 characters from the operator of its relational comparison (no comparison of the four crates is that long). An exclusion pins the text of its limit's expression. In the four crates a constant that the expression names is pinned too, as a term; an associated constant of a type (`Header::SIZE`), a constant of a crate outside the workspace and a value a function computes are not followed. A constant that another source of the workspace defines is scanned where it is defined when the code of the four crates names it: in a compared position, bare or behind a module path (also under the name a `use` of the file gives it), or in the defining expression of a scanned limit. The name stands for every integer constant of that name in a production source the naming crate can reach: any item of its own crate (a skipped directory) and a `pub` item of a workspace crate it depends on, directly or through other workspace crates. Each is a listed bound or excluded with a pinned expression, its terms are followed from its own source, and `--mutate` changes it. The resolution is by name, so each reachable crate that defines the name is scanned. Not seen there: an associated constant of a type of another crate (`Shape::SIZE`), a constant another crate re-exports under a new name, the root of a binary target and a source only test builds compile. The consensus core, the IVM and its ABI and the P2P layer are scanned by name and, like every other crate of the workspace, for the constants the four crates name.

It bounds the policy, not a quantity on the path; each policy field it caps is a bound above with its own value.

Codec-internal decode guards (archive length, nesting depth, header padding, varint width). Each chain bound above is measured on the framed encoding and is far below them; they never decide admission.

A decoder-internal field ceiling derived from a listed payload bound (the proof-box and verifying-key payload ceilings) plus its length prefix; it admits nothing the listed bound refuses.
Shape bounds of the Ed25519 batch-verification opcode payload, inside the guest memory and gas budgets; M.1 inventories the opcode's semantics.
Connection, send-queue and gossip fan-out capacity of the P2P layer: local back-pressure that delays or drops a delivery. It bounds no frame, transaction or block.
Largest number of transactions in one gossip batch: a local delivery batch size. The frame that carries the batch is bounded by transport.max_frame_bytes_tx_gossip.

literals.what: Literal comparisons of the `comparisons` scopes that no listed bound owns. A literal comparison is a comparison with `<`, `<=`, `>` or `>=` (also written as a method: `.lt`, `.le`, `.gt`, `.ge`), a capping call (`.min`, `.max`, `.clamp`, `.take`, `.truncate`), either of the two called as a function, bare or behind any path (`cmp::max(a, b)`, `u32::clamp(n, 2, 64)`), or a range tested with `.contains`, that holds an integer literal of `minimum` or more. Where the literal is a whole operand, argument or range end (also a product or shift of literals, such as `4 * 1024 * 1024`), the recorded text is that operand, the operator and the literal (`value.len() > 4096`). Where it is only a part of what is compared (`len > MAX + 1024`, `len / 2 >= MAX`, `timeout > Duration::from_secs(30)`, an index as in `fields[7].len() > MAX`, a factor in the receiver of `.min`, `.max`, `.clamp` or a comparison method), the recorded text is the whole comparison, call or range, unless the text of another recorded site holds the literal already. The receiver of such a call is the whole method chain in front of it; where the literal stands above the last element of a chain broken across lines, the text starts at the head of the chain (`delta .saturating_mul(10_000) .saturating_div(current) .min(cap)`). A comparison inside an enforcement site of a listed bound belongs to that bound and needs no entry; the site must hold its text whole, so a shorter comparison that is only a part of the site's text is not owned by it. Every other one is recorded here as `text: count` of its file, where `count` is how often the text occurs whatever number of literals it holds, in a group whose reason says why it is not a resource bound of the transaction and proof path. A literal has no other user, so each entry is local to the place it is written. A changed literal, a removed comparison and a new one each fail the checker until the group is reviewed; `--propose` prints the entries to add.
literals.why: A comparison with 0 or 1 tests presence, emptiness, sign or a single item. It is not a size, count or work bound and is not scanned.

groups.reason: Block heights and generations compared with the first heights after genesis (2 is the first block that follows genesis): a reader that serves no evidence at the genesis height, a proof whose window opens after genesis, a generation that has a predecessor. They select which history exists and bound no size, count or work.

Minimums. A decoder that needs at least so many bytes before it reads a header or a magic number; a list that needs at least two or three entries (inputs, signers, endpoints, lineage steps, tally options, carriers); a configured value that must reach a least size. A minimum refuses too little: it is no byte, count or work ceiling. Where the minimum is the start of a tested range (`(2..=MAX).contains(..)`) or a sum of fixed widths (`37 + 16 + 2`), the whole comparison is recorded; a named ceiling at the end of such a range has its own entry (one is the listed rs16.max_chunk_count, read back from a stored certificate).

Value ranges of one numeric field: basis points (10,000), percent (100), per mille (1,000), parts per million (1,000,000) and decimal scales (18). A fraud score in basis points is compared with its denominator and with the first band threshold (1,000). They bound the value of a number, not a size. A ratio is also compared by cross-multiplication: a governance margin below five percent of the decisive ballots, and an oracle error share above its configured basis points. The relative change of a compute price parameter (cycles or egress per unit) is scaled to basis points and capped at the largest 16-bit value; the 10,000 of that scaling is recorded with the cap.

Durations compared with a literal, in milliseconds or seconds: lifetimes, ages, validity and quota windows, clock skews. A time window is not a byte, count or work bound. The same holds for a literal inside a compared or clamped duration (`Duration::from_secs(30)`, a quota window of 60,000 ms), for the doubling of a retry backoff under its cap, and for windows counted in blocks: an NFT offer or custody sale expires at most 1,000,000 blocks after it is made, and the join deadline of a game session is at most 300 blocks ahead.

Arithmetic of an encoding, a field or a fixed table. Bit accumulators of base-32, base-58 and base-64 codecs; ASCII, UTF-8 and UTF-16 code-unit ranges; DER length forms and object-identifier arcs; CBOR and tag ranges; IPv4 and IPv6 prefix lengths and reserved address blocks; HTTP status classes; calendar arithmetic; decimal digit counts; stage, phase, operation and state codes; and indexes into fixed-width tables and bitmaps. Each parses, builds or indexes one value and bounds no amount. Also the 3-to-4 expansion of base64 text, the four bytes a UTF-8 character takes at most, the width of a fixed header, word or length field added to an offset before it is compared with a length, and an index written inside a comparison (`fields[7].len() > MAX`, `times[3] - times[0] > skew`): there the limit that is compared has its own entry and the literal only selects the element. An index inside a clamped ratio (`top_sums[2]`) only selects the element as well.

A literal given to `.min`, `.max`, `.clamp`, `.take` or `.truncate`. The call clamps a value the code computed or cuts an iterator or list the code built, and refuses nothing where it is written: a pre-allocation hint or a preview length, the page window of a listing, the exponent of a retry backoff, a queue depth derived from a worker count, the bytes a reader takes for one field, the padding of a circuit row, a ratio clamped to its denominator, a height raised to the first block after genesis. Where a clamped value is later a bound, the comparison that refuses is elsewhere and is scanned there. One clamp is a structure cap: the fold arity of a STARK/FRI proof, clamped to 32 in crates/iroha_core_zk/src/stark.rs, belongs with the excluded structure caps of that verifier. A literal inside the clamped expression is recorded with the call: the two predecessors of a tip in `height.saturating_sub(2).max(1)`.

Committee and epoch geometry of the first release (specs/sumeragi.md, section 1): a voting committee has 3f + 1 members with f from 1 to 10, so at least 4 and at most 31, and an epoch has at least three blocks. They are the structure of the protocol, fixed with it. The wire ceiling of a signer set is the listed transport.max_committee_size (1,024), far above them. The fault bound f is written `(n - 1) / 3` where a readiness quorum of n - f is counted, and the KAGEMUSHA mint-finality committee has the same least size of 4.

Geometry of fixed circuits and gadgets in the proof crate: the arity of a confidential transfer (at most two inputs and two outputs), instance-column, carrier and row counts, limb byte and bit widths of field packings, the lengths of a DER signature (8 to 72 bytes) and of authenticator data that a gadget is built for, source and word indexes, const-generic size checks and compile-time assertions over unmeasured size estimates. The shape of a circuit is fixed with its verifying key; none is applied to a submitted transaction, block or proof as a byte, count or work limit. Literals that are part of such a comparison are of the same kind: the halves of the full rounds of a Poseidon permutation, the last compression round and the 8-byte length field of SHA-256 padding, the pair count of a FRI layer (half its domain), a 128-bit limb window, the 2^126 quotient radix and a 2^12 row estimate, the offsets of a DER signature inside a gadget, four reserved rows of an advice column, and a slot of a row counter that only test builds keep.

Field ceilings and exact ranges of single data-model records, each checked in the validator of that record: the length of a name, identifier, label, host name, chain or deployment identifier, nonce or abstract; the count of one list or map; the Merkle path depths of a FASTPQ source statement (32) and of a private-dataspace inclusion proof (256); entrypoint text, variant, message and capacity shapes of a contract interface; the canonical frame ceiling of one stream-token custody instruction; and quota ceilings of a gateway configuration. None is a transaction, block, frame or generic proof byte ceiling: those are listed bounds. A record that travels in a transaction is inside transaction.max_tx_bytes whatever these say.

Field ceilings and exact ranges of the KAGEMUSHA offline-cash product (data model and proof crate): the length of one original document, certificate, attestation, signature, token, account, package or identifier; the count of one list; a journal sequence, a history size and a tree depth. Each is checked where that record is decoded or admitted. They are shape limits of one product's own records, like its named constants excluded above. None is a transaction, block, frame or generic proof ceiling. Some are written as a named ceiling of the product with a fixed allowance: 1,024 bytes above a possession record for its archive, 64 KiB kept free below a Node Mint submission, 87 bytes added to a proof input before it is compared with the proof ceiling, a quarter of a frame for one of four clock originals, and 65,536-byte chunks of a journal. The named ceiling is excluded above; the allowance is pinned here.

Shape ceilings in the node, each of one record, file or loop: nesting depths (the private-instruction review, a recovery record, the fee-reward head tree); search and index ceilings in Kura's own files; ceilings on the configuration, paths and output of the read-only evidence reader and of the fee-reward evidence tool; snapshot field sizes; manifest and outcome shapes of a game session; request shapes of the retail-fee service; a ticket, a signer and a chain identifier; the execution results and outputs a driver retains; and the rejection-tail and self-claim instruction counts. Each is compared where it is written. None is a transaction, block, frame or generic proof byte ceiling.

Request, response and configuration shapes of Torii's HTTP, MCP, SoraFS, operator and bridge services: the length of one header value, token, nonce, URL, host name, label, identifier or query name; the count of one list; the body ceiling of one response; and ceilings on a service's own configuration values. Torii refuses one request or one configuration with them; no transaction, block or proof is judged. Transaction submission is bounded by the listed transport.torii_max_content_len and transaction.torii_app_api_payload_max_bytes.

Test support that a non-test build compiles only with a test feature of its crate (`iroha-core-tests`, `test-fixtures`, `test-utils`, `kagemusha-real-proof-harness`) or as a fixture tool in src/bin: fixture builders, the certified test chain and a qualification harness. Nothing a node receives is compared with them. The ADDR-2 compliance-vector generator of the data model is compiled into the library for the example binary and the CLI; it shortens an encoding by four bytes to build a negative vector.

A fixed factor written beside a named limit, where the amount compared is a multiple of what the limit counts: the hex text of a byte string is twice its bytes (the autoscale committee and a MUSUBI account identifier); an operation history advances by two revisions for each admitted operation, so its revision ceiling is twice the operation ceiling (SoraFS topology, final promotion and stream-token authority); a lane-geometry transition lists at most two operations for each binding; the effective World authority catalog is a baseline plus runtime additions, each within the catalog ceiling; the NFT preview of the IVM host queues two instructions for each NFT; and the journal share of a native-finality response budget is two of its eight units, clamped to the named journal ceiling. Each named limit is a shape limit of its own record and is excluded above. The factor is pinned here because changing it moves the ceiling while the constant stays the same.

Unit conversion beside a compared time. Block, ledger and record times in milliseconds are divided by 1,000 before they are compared with a timestamp, an epoch or a validity bound in seconds; a lifetime in seconds is multiplied by 1,000 before it clamps a remaining time in milliseconds; and milliseconds are rounded up to whole seconds for the CPU limit of a sanitizer process. The literal converts a unit. What is compared is a time, never a byte, count or work bound. The same rounding gives the whole seconds of a Retry-After header, at least 1.

Fractions and multiples of an amount one node computed or was configured with: a drand quorum must be more than half of the configured endpoints; half of the open-file budget, a quarter of the dispatch slots and half of a scan's time budget are set aside; an expiry index is compacted at twice its capacity; a scan budget is eight times the page limit, under its named ceiling; a decode allowance is at most half of the fanout's; half of the history-checkpoint slots, up to a named capacity, are recent ones; a name suggestion tolerates an edit distance of a quarter of the name, at least 2; and a query scans the assets directly when its selection covers an eighth of them. Each splits or scales a local amount that is bounded where it is configured or computed and decides no validity: none is a transaction, block, frame or proof ceiling. Likewise the age budget of the queue-pressure heuristic is three block times and a resolver bloom filter takes 16 bits for each expected item, each clamped between two named values, and a staging buffer of the authority registry doubles its capacity up to its maximum.

SCCP emergency-pause panel record geometry: a minimum ten citizens and between twice and three times the configured valid panel seats. These exact record-shape checks confer no authentication or authority and do not replace generic transaction/proof ceilings.

Deterministic SCCP post-execution destination clearance visits at most the first64 pending generations in canonical order and may change committed State/events. This product-maintenance count (L5) is not local scheduling and does not bound inner route/revision work. It is separate from generic transaction/proof admission ceilings and confers no authority for unfinished generation/anchor deletion.
